entry: English actor, comedian and musician. Laurie gained recognition in the comedy double act Fry and Laurie with [[Stephen Fry]], which included the BBC sketch series *A Bit of Fry & Laurie*. From 2004 to 2012 he starred as Dr. Gregory House in the Fox medical drama *House*, earning two Golden Globe Awards. He later won a Golden Globe for the TV series *The Night Manager*. Laurie released the blues albums *Let Them Talk* (2011) and *Didn't It Rain* (2013), and wrote the novel *The Gun Seller* (1996). He was appointed OBE in 2007 and CBE in 2018, both for services to drama.

Venezuelan military officer and politician, president of [[Venezuela]] from 1999 to 2013. Chávez led an unsuccessful 1992 coup against the government of Carlos Andrés Pérez, was imprisoned, and was pardoned in 1994. He founded the Fifth Republic Movement, won the 1998 presidential election, and was reelected in 2000 and 2006. He nationalized key industries and funded the Bolivarian missions with record oil revenues. Oil income brought temporary gains in poverty reduction, literacy and income equality, mainly between 2003 and 2007, but structural inequalities changed little. Critics argue that price controls and deficit spending were unsustainable and that the economy faltered as oil prices fell. His government suppressed the press and critics. Chávez described himself as a Marxist. He died in [[Caracas]] before his fourth-term inauguration, and his ideas form the basis of Chavismo.

Dutch jurist and humanist, also known as Hugo de Groot. Imprisoned in Loevestein Castle in 1619 for his part in religious disputes in the Dutch Republic, he escaped hidden in a book chest and wrote most of his major works in exile in France. His *De jure belli ac pacis* (*On the Law of War and Peace*, 1625), dedicated to [[Louis XIII]] of France, argued for rational limits on warfare and derived legal obligations from human nature and reason. He defended freedom of the seas in *Mare liberum* and is called the "father of [[International law|international law]]". Hedley Bull called him a possible intellectual father of the [[Peace of Westphalia]]. His Arminian theology contributed seeds for later movements such as [[Methodism]] and [[Pentecostalism]].

French Protestants of the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition. The term was in use by about 1550 and may derive from Besançon Hugues, a burgomaster who defended [[Geneva]] from Catholic Savoy. Huguenots made up as much as 10% of the French population on the eve of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572. Catholic hostility grew, and the [[French Wars of Religion]] ended with the Edict of Nantes in 1598, which granted substantial religious and military autonomy. [[Louis XIV]] revoked Protestant rights in the Edict of Fontainebleau in 1685, and Dragonnades forced conversion or flight. Persecution officially ended with the Edict of Versailles in 1787, and the revolutionary [[Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen]] of 1789 gave Protestants equal rights. In 2013 the Reformed Church of France merged with the Lutheran church to form the United Protestant Church of France.

Semi-legendary Chinese Chan Buddhist master, traditionally the sixth patriarch of Chan. According to tradition, Huineng was an uneducated layman who attained awakening upon hearing the [[Diamond Sutra]] while selling firewood. The fifth patriarch, Hongren, supposedly chose him as successor over the publicly favored Shenxiu. Huineng is regarded as the founder of the Southern Chan school, which teaches sudden enlightenment. The *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*, said to record his teachings, was compiled over centuries and attributed to a disciple. Twentieth-century scholarship suggests that the biography was likely invented by the monk Shenhui, who claimed to be one of Huineng's disciples.

Swiss theologian and leader of the [[Reformation]] in Switzerland. He studied at Vienna and Basel, served as a pastor in Glarus and Einsiedeln, and was influenced by [[Erasmus]]. In 1519 he became people's priest at the Grossmünster in [[Zurich]], where he preached reform, attacked fasting during Lent and promoted clerical marriage. In 1525 he introduced a new communion liturgy to replace the Mass. He clashed with the Anabaptists, who were persecuted, and historians debate whether he made Zurich a theocracy. His alliance of Reformed cantons divided the Swiss Confederation along religious lines. At the Marburg Colloquy he agreed with [[Martin Luther]] on many doctrines but not on the Real Presence of Christ in the [[Eucharist]]. In 1531 his alliance's food blockade failed, and he died on the battlefield.

Mongol ruler who founded the Ilkhanate in Persia. A grandson of [[Genghis Khan]], he was a brother of [[Kublai Khan]] and Möngke Khan. Möngke charged him with conquering the remaining Muslim states of southwestern Asia. He destroyed the Nizari Ismaili state and accepted the surrender of its Alamut fortress in 1256. In 1258 his army besieged [[Baghdad]], which surrendered and was sacked, ending the [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. The caliph was captured, and the Grand Library was destroyed. Estimates of the dead range from about 90,000 to a million. Damascus was also weakened, shifting Islamic influence to the [[Mamluk Sultanate]] in Cairo.

Fictional superhero in American comic books published by [[Marvel Comics]]. Created by writer [[Stan Lee]] and artist [[Jack Kirby]], the Hulk first appeared in *The Incredible Hulk* in May 1962. He is the green-skinned alter ego of physicist Bruce Banner, who is transformed by emotional stress after accidental exposure to [[Gamma ray|gamma rays]] during an experimental bomb detonation. The Hulk's strength is usually proportionate to his anger. Live-action portrayals include Bill Bixby and [[Lou Ferrigno]] in the 1978 television series *The Incredible Hulk*, Eric Bana in the 2003 film *Hulk*, and Edward Norton and then Mark Ruffalo in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]].

American [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestler]] and media personality, born Terry Gene Bollea. He won six WWF/WWE Championships and headlined eight of the first nine WrestleMania events in the 1980s. In 1994 he joined World Championship Wrestling, won its world heavyweight title six times, and led the New World Order. He also appeared in films such as *Rocky III* (1982) and *No Holds Barred* (1989). In 1994 he admitted to using anabolic [[Steroid|steroids]] dating back to 1976. After Gawker published portions of a sex tape in 2012, Hogan sued the company, which was found liable and later declared bankruptcy.

Composite index of life expectancy, education and per capita income, used to rank countries into four tiers of human development. Pakistani economist Mahbub ul-Haq devised it for the United Nations Development Programme's annual Human Development Reports, begun in 1990. The index is anchored in Amartya Sen's work on human capabilities. It does not account for net wealth per capita, which tends to lower the ranking of developed countries such as the [[G7]]. The 2010 report introduced an inequality-adjusted index.

External opening of the rectum, located in the intergluteal cleft. It is the final part of the [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal tract]]. Two sphincters control defecation: the internal anal sphincter is involuntary, and the external anal sphincter is voluntary. The anus is a site of potential infections and conditions such as [[Hemorrhoid|hemorrhoids]] and cancer. With [[Anal sex]], it plays a role in sexuality, a practice that is illegal in some countries. Some sexually transmitted infections, including HIV/AIDS, can spread through anal sex.

Central organ of the human nervous system. With the spinal cord, it forms the central nervous system and consists of the [[Cerebrum]], brainstem and [[Cerebellum]]. The cerebrum has two hemispheres, each covered by a gray matter [[Cerebral cortex|cerebral cortex]] and divided into four lobes. The frontal lobe is associated with executive functions such as self-control, planning and reasoning, while the occipital lobe is dedicated to vision. Language is associated with the left hemisphere and visual-spatial ability with the right. The brain contains more than 86 billion [[Neuron|neurons]] and a roughly equal number of other cells. It is protected by the skull and cerebrospinal fluid, and is susceptible to [[Stroke]], Parkinson's disease, [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer's disease]] and multiple sclerosis.

Practice of humans eating the flesh or organs of other humans. Anatomically modern humans, Neanderthals and Homo antecessor practiced it to some extent in the Pleistocene. It occurred in ancient Egypt and Rome and during severe famines. The word cannibal derives from the Island Caribs of the [[Lesser Antilles]]. Cannibalism is documented in Fiji, the Amazon Basin, the Congo and among the Māori of New Zealand. Consuming body parts or blood for medicine was popular in early modern Europe, peaking in the 17th century. Starvation led to cannibalism in cases such as the [[Holodomor]] (1932–1933). Reports by outsiders, especially during colonialism, require critical examination. Cannibalism was still practiced in Papua New Guinea as of 2012, for cultural reasons.

[[Gastrointestinal tract|Gastrointestinal tract]] and accessory organs that break down food for absorption. The accessory organs include the tongue, salivary glands, [[Pancreas]], [[Liver]] and gallbladder. Digestion proceeds in cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases. Saliva contains amylase, and the [[Stomach]] mixes food with gastric juice containing gastric acid. Peristalsis moves food along the tract. Most digestion takes place in the [[Small intestine]], where nutrients are absorbed. The large intestine reabsorbs water and some minerals, and waste leaves through the anus.

Sensory organ of the [[Visual system|visual system]] that responds to visible light. The eye is approximately spherical and typically about 24 mm (0.94 in) in diameter. The cornea provides most of its optical power, and the iris controls how much light enters through the pupil. The crystalline [[Lens]] focuses the remaining light onto the retina. The retina contains approximately 120 million rods and 6 million cones. Rods respond to low-intensity light and produce grayscale images, while cones respond to high-intensity light and perceive color. Photosensitive ganglion cells help regulate the hormone melatonin and [[Circadian rhythm|circadian rhythm]]. Signals reach the brain via the optic nerve.

Complete set of [[DNA]] sequences in humans, comprising 22 autosomes and the X and Y sex [[Chromosome|chromosomes]], plus a small genome within mitochondria. The standard reference genome, GRCh38.p14 (July 2023), contains approximately 3.1 billion base pairs. The human reference genome contains between 19,000 and 20,000 protein-coding genes, but coding DNA makes up only about 1–2% of the genome. In 2000, scientists reported sequencing 88% of the genome. The Y chromosome, consisting of 62,460,029 base pairs, was completely sequenced in January 2022. Individuals differ by about 0.1% of their sequences. Humans differ from their closest living relatives, the [[Chimpanzee|chimpanzee]] and [[Bonobo|bonobo]], by about 1.1% in fixed single-nucleotide variants.

Branch of geography, also known as anthropogeography, that studies how people interact with their environments. It examines spatial relationships between human communities, cultures, economies and lifestyles, using qualitative and quantitative methods. The field draws on sociology, anthropology, economics and environmental science. The first professor of geography in the United Kingdom was appointed in 1883. [[London School of Economics|London School of Economics]] appointed Halford John Mackinder professor in 1922. John Snow's 1854 map of a [[Cholera]] outbreak is probably one of the earliest examples of health geography. Environmental determinism, popularized by Carl Ritter in the 19th century, was later criticized as a means to justify racism and imperialism. The 1960s quantitative revolution introduced statistics and [[Geographic information system|geographic information systems]].

Changes to biophysical environments, ecosystems and natural resources caused directly or indirectly by humans. Modifying the environment for society contributes to global warming, ocean acidification, mass extinction and biodiversity loss. Drivers include population growth, rapid economic growth, overconsumption, pollution and [[Deforestation|deforestation]]. Human-caused impacts have increased significantly since the [[Industrial Revolution]] in the 1700s, but prehistoric peoples also cleared forests, hunted wildlife, grew crops and herded livestock. Paul Crutzen introduced the term [[Anthropocene]] in the mid-1970s.

Intellectual capability of humans, marked by complex cognitive feats and high levels of motivation and self-awareness. Humans learn, form concepts, reason, recognize patterns, plan, solve problems and use language. Psychometrics assesses it with [[Intelligence quotient|IQ]] tests. Scholars debate whether subcategories such as emotional intelligence are distinct forms, and whether intelligence is fixed at birth or malleable. A 2018 metastudy called education the "most consistent, robust, and durable method" known for raising intelligence. Psychologist Wayne Weiten argues that IQ tests validly measure the intelligence needed for academic work, but that their validity as broader measures is questionable. Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences is based on studies of normal and gifted individuals and of people with brain damage.

Lower limb of the human body, including the thigh, knee, lower leg and foot. Each leg contains thirty bones, including the femur, tibia and [[Fibula]]. The patella, the largest sesamoid bone in the body, lies in front of the knee. Human legs evolved for efficient [[Bipedalism|bipedal]] gait, which other primates sustain only briefly and at great energy cost. Leg length is 111% of trunk length in [[Orangutan|orangutans]], 128% in chimpanzees and 171% in humans. The gluteal muscles, knee extensors and calf muscles are adapted to bipedalism. Female legs generally have greater hip anteversion, while male legs have longer femur and tibial lengths.

Fundamental dispositions and characteristics that humans are said to have naturally, including ways of thinking, feeling and acting. The concept is central to philosophy and relates to the nature versus nurture debate. [[Aristotle]] held that human nature was fixed and goal-directed. According to Aristotle, the philosophical study of human nature began with [[Socrates]], who turned philosophy toward how humans should best live. In early modern times [[Thomas Hobbes|Hobbes]], [[John Locke|Locke]] and [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau|Rousseau]] argued for relative malleability, and Rousseau held that people cannot know what their nature permits them to be. [[Charles Darwin|Darwin]]'s theory of evolution showed that human ancestors were not like humans today. Since the early 19th century, Freud, Marx, Nietzsche and Sartre have also argued against a fixed human nature.

Condition in which human populations may become too large for their environment or resources to sustain in the long term. Since 1804 the global population has grown from 1 billion to 8 billion. Annual growth peaked at 2.1% in 1968 and has since dropped to 1.1%. United Nations projections expect 9.7 billion people in 2050, peaking at around 10.4 billion in the 2080s. Paul Ehrlich's 1968 book *The Population Bomb* popularized the concern. Economist Julian Simon argued that humans are "the ultimate resource" and that [[Green Revolution|agricultural innovation]] outpaced population pressure. Critics argue that the concern is overstated and that it ignores [[Poverty|poverty]] and overconsumption.

Infection caused by a DNA virus of the Papillomaviridae family. Most infections cause no symptoms, and 90% resolve within two years. Persistent infections can cause [[Wart|warts]] or precancerous lesions that increase the risk of cancers of the cervix, vulva, vagina, penis, anus and throat. Nearly all cervical cancer is due to HPV, and HPV16 and HPV18 account for 70% of cases. More than 40 types spread through sexual contact, and HPV is the most common [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infection]] globally. It is not killed by common hand sanitizers or disinfectants. Vaccines prevent the most common types. Cervical cancer caused an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths in 2020.

External male sex organ through which males urinate and ejaculate. The penis has three columns of erectile tissue: two corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum, through which the urethra passes. An erection is the stiffening of the penis during sexual arousal, though spontaneous erections often occur during adolescence and sleep. In the flaccid state the [[Foreskin|foreskin]] covers the glans. Age and flaccid size do not accurately predict erect length. The penis is homologous to the [[Clitoris]] in females. [[Circumcision]] is among the common body modifications.

Ritual killing of one or more humans, usually to please or appease gods, rulers or ancestors. Many societies practiced it from prehistoric times, and it became less common across Africa, Europe and Asia in the [[Iron Age]]. Classical antiquity considered it barbaric, but it continued in the Americas until European colonization. The [[Aztecs]] reported killing about 80,400 prisoners over four days at the 1487 rededication of the Great Pyramid of Tenochtitlan. Retainer sacrifice killed servants so they could serve a ruler in the afterlife. Modern secular laws treat human sacrifice as murder.
